story:
Kai sat at the art table. The sun felt warm, like summer coming in the window. He had red, blue, yellow and green paint. He wanted to make a traffic light for the toy cars.

But which color goes on top? Kai tapped the brush. He thought about walking to the park with Grandma. At the corner, the light turned red. The cars stopped. Then it turned green. The cars got to zip past.

"Red means stop," Kai said to himself. "Green means go." So he painted red on top. He painted green on the bottom. He painted yellow in the middle, just like the real one.

Then Mia drove a toy car across the table. Kai held up his paper. "Red!" he called. Mia stopped her car fast. "Green!" Kai said. The little car zipped down the table and around the paint cups. "Again!" said Mia. Kai smiled and turned his paper back to red.

"One more time," said Mia, "then a blue car too."

activity: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
story:
Emile was at Grandma's house. It was time for lunch. Grandma set the big bowl on the table. She poured warm soup into the cups.

"Emile, would you like to say grace?" asked Grandma.

Emile looked at the soup. Emile looked at his shoes. He did not know what to say. He hid his face in his hat.

"That's okay," said Grandma. "Everyone holds hands. We say thank you."

Emile peeked out from the hat. Grandma held out her hand. Emile took it.

"Thank you for the soup," Emile said, very small.

"Yay!" said Grandma. She clapped.

Emile sat up tall. "Thank you for the soup!" he said again, very big.

Grandma laughed. "Now we eat."

Emile drank his warm soup. He was still holding the hat.

Sienna looked at her hands. They had dog fur on them. Yucky hands. She ran to the sink. The sink was not far from the table. Mom turned on the water.

Sienna pumped the soap. "Bubbles!" she said. She rubbed her hands. Then she counted. "One, two, three, four, five." Mom counted too. "Six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Sienna kept going. "Eleven, twelve, thirteen, fourteen, fifteen." Her hands were slippery. "Sixteen, seventeen, eighteen, nineteen, twenty!"

Sienna looked at her hands. The fur was gone. The bubbles lifted away down the drain. Clean hands! Mom gave her a warm sandwich. Sienna took a bite. Then she held up her hand to high five Mom. A tiny bubble was still on her thumb. "Look, Mom! One bubble missed the drain!" said Sienna. Mom laughed. "That one wants to stay for lunch," said Mom. Sienna popped it with one finger.

Asher sat in the big barber chair. It went up, up, up! "My first haircut!" he said. The barber, Mr. Sam, picked up his scissors. Snip, snip, snip.

story:

story:
Mia was ready for bed. But her toy horse was missing. She looked under the bed. No horse. She looked in the toy box. No horse. Mia's face went hot. She stamped her foot. "My horse is gone!" she said. She felt angry.

Outside the window, soft snow was falling. Mama came in and sat down. "Let's take big slow breaths," said Mama. "Like this." Mama breathed in slowly. Mia breathed in slowly too. Then she let the breath out, slow and long. They did it again. Mia's tummy felt soft now. Her feet felt still. "Where could he be?" asked Mia. Mama said, "Look by the pillow." There was the horse, tucked under the blanket, all cozy.

Mia hugged him tight. She felt happy. Mama turned off the light. The snow kept falling outside. "Night-night, horse," whispered Mia.

story:
Grandma was coming on a plane. She would stay at Harrison's house for a whole week. Harrison packed his toy truck. He packed his big red ball. "Grandma can play with me," he said.

Dad drove them to the airport. They stood by the doors where people come off the plane. Harrison watched the doors very hard. A man came out. "Grandma!" cried Harrison. "No," said Dad. "Look again." A lady came out with a big coat. "Grandma!" cried Harrison. "Not yet," said Dad, and he laughed softly. "Keep watching." Then Harrison saw one shoe. Then two feet. Then a red bag. Then a face he knew. "Grandma!" Grandma opened her arms wide. Harrison ran to her. Her coat felt soft and smelled like flowers. "My big boy," said Grandma. "I heard you calling me."

At home, Grandma made tea. Dad held the hot cup. Harrison gave Grandma his red ball. She rolled it with her foot, back and forth, back and forth. "Again," said Harrison. "Again, again!" Grandma rolled the ball and laughed and laughed.

story:
Benjamin ran to the playground. He wanted to find his friend Mia. He looked by the swings. He looked by the slide. Then he saw her in the sand. She was holding a toy farm with little cows.

Mia's mouth was turned down. Her eyebrows were scrunchy. Benjamin watched her face. She looked sad.

"What is wrong?" he asked.

"My cow is lost," said Mia. "It fell in the sand."

Benjamin dug in the sand with both hands. The sand was soft and cool. Then he felt something hard. It was the little cow!

Mia's mouth turned up into a big smile. She jumped up and down. "You found it!" she said.

Just then a big dog barked by the fence. It sounded scary. Mia hid behind Benjamin. Her eyes were wide.

Benjamin held her hand. The dog's owner called it away. The dog trotted off, wagging its tail.

"That dog is gone now," said Benjamin.

Mia laughed. She gave him a cow from the farm. "You keep this one," she said. "You are my best digger."

Benjamin put the cow in his pocket. Then they built a big red barn together in the sand.

story:
Sarah sat at a big table in the restaurant. A big screen glowed on the wall. Mom and Dad and Uncle Ben were there too. Everyone was watching the game.

The red team ran with the ball. Sarah clapped her hands. "Go, go!" she shouted. The blue team scored a goal. Everyone at the table jumped up. They cheered and clapped for the blue team. Sarah looked around. She had clapped for the red team! She laughed and laughed. "Oops," she said. "I clapped for the wrong team."

Sarah watched the screen some more. Now the blue team ran fast. A player kicked the ball. It went in! Sarah jumped up with everyone. She clapped and cheered too. "Blue team!" she called. Uncle Ben gave her a high five. A waiter brought fries, and Sarah shared them with her cousin. "Sorry, I ate the big one," her cousin said. Sarah giggled and took the next one.

story:
Henry went to the hospital with Dad. Mom had a new baby. The baby was Henry's little sister. She was very small.

The baby began to cry. "Why is she crying?" Henry asked. Henry thought and thought. He remembered when sand got in his shoe. He could not say "ow." So he cried too. Maybe the baby could not talk yet. Maybe crying was her way of asking.

Henry tried one thing. He gave her a soft toy. The baby kept crying. Henry tried another thing. He held her little hand. The baby still cried. Then Mom picked her up. Mom gave the baby milk. The baby stopped crying. She made a small sound. She fell asleep.

"She was hungry," said Mom. "She told us by crying." Henry gave his sister a kiss on her head. She was so young and so small. "I will listen," Henry said. "Cry, and I will come."

Brielle sat in her reading nook with a big alphabet chart. She wanted to learn every letter. She pointed at A. "A says ahh," she said. She pointed at B. "B says buh." Then she got to a letter that looked like a stick and a loop. She did not know it. She felt mad and tossed her sock at the chart.

Her brother came in. "Try counting them," he said. Brielle pointed and counted. "One, two, three..." She went slowly. Some letters looked alike. She went back and tried again. She got all the way to the end. "Twenty-six!" she said. "There are twenty-six letters!"

She picked up her sock and put it away. Then she looked at the stick-and-loop letter again. "M," she read. "M says mmm, like mmmilk!" Her brother clapped. Brielle pointed to one more letter and smiled. "N. That one is next."

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Kayden wanted to go to the library. "Is it library day?" he asked. Mom smiled. "Yes, it is today." Kayden jumped up and down. "Today means now?" he asked. "Yes," said Mom. "Today is the day that is happening right now."

But first they had to wait. Mom had to wash the dishes. Kayden watched the water splash. He heard a plane fly over the house. It made a big sound in the sky. Then the plane was gone. "Later we go," said Mom. "After the dishes."

Kayden felt shy about waiting. He wanted to cry a little. Yesterday he had waited too. Yesterday, Grandma had read him a book. That was yesterday, not now. Mom finished the dishes. "Now we go!" she said.

At the library, Kayden picked three books. "Can we come again?" he asked. "Tomorrow," said Mom. "Tomorrow is after today." Kayden held her hand tight. They walked home with the books. "Tonight I will read them," he said. Mom laughed and kissed his head.

story:
Elizabeth was at the farm with Grandpa. The pigs needed to bathe in the warm sun. "Let's play a game," said Grandpa. "Tell me your five senses." Elizabeth held up one little finger. "One! I see with my eyes!" She saw a black cow. "Two! I hear with my ears!" She heard the cow say moo.

Grandpa pointed to a rose. "Now smell this one." Elizabeth sniffed with her nose. "Mmm, sweet!" Then she sniffed a mint leaf. "Ooh, tingly!" She sniffed Grandpa's boot. "P.U.! Stinky!" Grandpa laughed and laughed. "Three!" said Elizabeth. "I smell with my nose!"

She touched a soft bunny. "Four! I touch with my hands!" Then they shared apple slices. "Five! I taste with my mouth!" Grandpa held up a flower near Elizabeth's nose. "One more sniff?" Elizabeth took a big sniff. "Sweet, sweet, sweet!" she said. Grandpa clapped his hands.

Lucas sat at the kitchen table. He had a big new pencil. He wanted to write his name!

"First letter is L," said Mom. "One line down. One line across."

Lucas held the pencil tight. He made a big L. He made a u. He made a c. He made a s. "L-U-C-A-S," he said out loud. Soon he had five letters!

Then his lines got fat and fuzzy. His last S looked like a fat fuzzy worm. "Oh no," said Lucas. He tapped the pencil tip. It was dull.

Mom took the pencil. She turned it in the sharpener. Lucas watched from his chair.

The tip was pointy again! Lucas wrote his name once more. The letters were thin and beautiful. "Look, Mom! One, two, three, four, five letters!"

"Let's tell Dad this story at dinner," said Mom. Lucas grinned and wrote his name again.

Then he saw something odd. A tiny ant was on the slide. It crawled up. Then it slid all the way down. The ant did it again.

"Look, ant," said Bennett. "You go up too!"

Bennett climbed up once more. He held his arms out wide. The sun felt hot on his hands. The slide felt cool and smooth.

"Wee!" he called. Down he went, right past the ant.

The little ant waved its legs, as if to say hello.

Josephine was at Mia's house. Mia had a tablet. Josephine wanted to draw on it.

Mia's mom showed her how. "Push the round button with your finger," she said. Josephine pushed it. The screen lit up. Her push made the light come on!

"Now tap the little paint pot," said Mia. Josephine tapped it. The drawing app opened. She drew a thin blue line. Then she drew a big sun.

"I win," said Josephine. "I made a sun!"

Then the screen went black. Josephine's tummy felt tight. "Did I break it?" she asked.

"No," said Mia's mom. "It is just tired." She plugged the charger into the tablet. A small battery picture showed up on the screen.

"It needs to eat," said Mia.

Josephine watched the battery picture fill up a little. Then Mia's mom put the tablet on the shelf. "It rests while it charges," she said.

"When can we draw again?" asked Josephine.

"After snack time," said Mia's mom. "Then you can push the button yourself."

They ate apple slices at the table. Josephine looked at the shelf. The tablet sat still, with its thin white cord.

After snack, Josephine pushed the button with her finger. The screen lit up again.

"It came back," she said. "Hello, sun!"

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Sophie sat at the dinner table. She wanted the bread, but it was far away. She reached and reached. The basket did not move.

"Papa, we went to the park tomorrow," said Sophie.

"Tomorrow?" asked Papa. He passed her the bread.

Sophie took a bite and thought. "No, not tomorrow," she said. "It already happened. It was yesterday. Yesterday we went to the park."

"Yes," said Mama. "And today we are eating dinner. Now the bread is in your hand."

"Tomorrow I want to go again," said Sophie. "Tomorrow is not here yet."

"That is a long wait," said Mama.

Sophie looked at her cup. She looked at the flower in the middle of the table. She had picked it on their walk, the last one in the yard.

"Can we have bread again tomorrow?" she asked.

"We can," said Papa. "Bread takes time. Mama will make it later tonight."

Sophie ate slowly. Tomorrow the park would come. Tomorrow the bread would come too.

"Now I will eat my peas," said Sophie.

Mom slid the paper over. "Try starting at the left," she said. Jackson tapped the left side with his finger. Then he began there. J, a, c, k, s, o, n. It all fit!

Then the pencil made a surprise. A wet spoon had sat on the paper. Where Jackson wrote, the letters turned dark blue! Jackson laughed. "My name is blue!" he said. He opened the door and called, "Dad, come see!"

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Arlo went to the park today. Yesterday it had rained. Today the sun was out. The slide was still wet, so Arlo had to wait.

"I want to slide now," said Arlo.

"Not yet," said Grandma. "Later, when it is dry."

Arlo waited. He watched the sun shine on the slide. Soon the slide was dry. He grabbed the rail and climbed up. Down he went, fast and happy.

Grandma sat on a bench like a desk, with her book on her lap. "Tomorrow we can come back," she said.

"Tomorrow is soon," said Arlo.

"Do you know how long a week is?" asked Grandma. "We will come back for a whole week of visits."

Arlo held up one hand. He counted his fingers. "One, two, three, four, five." He ran out of fingers. He looked at his other hand. He counted on. "Six, seven."

"A week has seven days," said Arlo. He wiggled all seven fingers.

At home, Arlo drew seven suns on his paper, one for each park day. The last one he drew snowy, with tiny dots of white. "That day will be cold," he said.

"Maybe," said Grandma, smiling.

Arlo put the paper by his bed. "Now I sleep," he said. "Tomorrow, sun number one."

Grandma tucked him in and turned out the light.

activity: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
story:
Matteo held his grandma's hand. They walked into the big hall with soft seats. People were quiet there. A kind man in robes smiled at them. After the quiet time, everyone went to a long table. There were bowls of warm rice.

Grandma sat down next to Matteo. "Now we say itadakimasu," she said. "We say it before we eat. It gives thanks for the food." Matteo looked at the rice. He wanted to say it just right. He tried. "Ita... daki... moose!" A boy across the table giggled. Matteo's face felt warm.

Grandma said the word slowly, one part at a time. "Ee-ta-da-kee-mas." Matteo said it with her. Once. Twice. Three times. On the third try, his mouth got it. The whole table said itadakimasu together. Then everyone picked up their chopsticks and spoons.

Matteo took a bite of rice. It tasted good. He drew a picture after lunch with a crayon. He drew the bowl and grandma and the word in wobbly letters. A boy bumped his arm and said, "Nice picture." Matteo smiled. "Want to say it with me next time?" he asked.

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
story:
Maverick wanted his own little garden. Grandma gave him three seeds and a small spot of soil. He patted the seeds down into the dirt. "Now grow," he said.

Every morning Maverick came to look. He saw dirt. He saw a worm. He saw an old piece of wood. He did not see a plant. "Where is my plant?" he asked. "Keep looking," said Grandma. The sun felt hot on his hat. Maverick slipped his hand into the cool soil to check the seeds. Still quiet. Still brown. He looked again the next day. And the next day. And the day after that.

Then one morning, something tiny and green stood up in the dirt. It was small as his finger. "Grandma! A sprout! A sprout came up!" Grandma knelt down beside him. "Yes," she said. "That is a sprout." Maverick smiled at the little green sprout. "Grow big," he whispered. He gave it a small drink of water from his cup.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Eliana went to the store with Grandma. She held Grandma's hand. "Stay close to me," said Grandma. Elian stayed close.

In the store there was a big soup pot. Steam came up from it. Eliana felt warm air on her face. "Hot," said Grandma. "We look with our eyes. We do not touch." Eliana looked and looked. One, two, three puffs of steam went up.

Eliana saw a small box on the floor. It said "matches" on it. She did not touch it. "Grandma, look," she said. Grandma picked it up. "Good girl. Matches and lighters are for grown-ups," said Grandma. She put the box in her pocket. Then they found a kind lady in a white coat. She was a doctor buying bread. "Hello, Eliana," she said. "Would you like a taste of jam?"

Eliana tasted apple jam. It was cold and sweet. "Yum," said Eliana. Grandma smiled. At the checkout, Eliana helped put apples on the belt. One apple, two apples, three apples. The lady said, "What a clean and helpful girl." Grandma held out her hand. Eliana took it. "Home we go," said Grandma. Eliana waved to the doctor. "Bye-bye, apple jam," said Eliana.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Emilia stood at the park gate. Today was a beautiful summer day. Yesterday it had rained, and the swings were wet. Now the swings were dry.

"Can I swing now?" Emilia asked.

"Yes, now," said Mom. "But later we go home for lunch."

Emilia pumped her legs. She went high, then low. The sun made her shadow grow tall on the ground.

"When is later?" she asked. "Is it now?"

Mom held up her phone. "See this little clock? It shows what time it is. When the short hand points to the twelve, it is lunch time."

Emilia looked at the little clock. The hand was not at the twelve yet. She slid down and ran to the sandbox.

"Not twelve yet," she said. "So I can dig now."

She filled her red bucket. She tipped it over. Out came a sand cake.

"Tomorrow we come back," said Mom.

"Tomorrow," said Emilia. She waved at the sandbox. "Bye, sand cake. Bye, park."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
story:
Grayson walked on the nature trail with Mama. He held a small bag of things to touch. Inside were a feather, a pinecone, and a soft purple blanket.

"I will make a puzzle," Grayson said. He put the three things on a flat rock. "Which ones are soft? Which one is rough?" He touched the feather with his finger. Soft. He touched the blanket. Soft, too. Then he touched the pinecone. It poked him a little. Rough!

"My skin can tell," Grayson said. He put the feather and the blanket on one side of the rock. He put the pinecone all by itself on the other side. Then he touched the pinecone again. Still rough. He touched the blanket again. Still soft.

A butterfly landed near the purple blanket. Grayson watched it open and close its wings. He heard a bird call from a tree. He sniffed the pine air. Then he picked up the feather and tickled his own nose.

"That tickles!" he said, and he laughed all the way down the trail.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: going on a family trip away from home
story:
Hannah sat on the train with Mama. The train went clickety-clack, clickety-clack. Hannah looked out the window. A cow stood in a green field. Then a little pig ran by the fence. "I see a pig!" said Hannah. "Same pig again," said Mama, laughing, because the train went around a bend.

They were going to the beach. Hannah wanted to splash in the big water. The train stopped. Daddy carried the bag. Grandma held Hannah's hand. They walked down to the sand. It was warm and soft. Hannah could hear the waves. Splash, splash, splash.

Hannah ran toward the water. Grandma called, "Wait for me!" Hannah stopped. She stood very still. The water went swish over her toes. Grandma came and stood right beside her. Then Hannah jumped. Splash! The water flew up. It got Grandma's dress all wet. Hannah laughed and jumped again. Grandma laughed too.

Mama spread out a towel. Hannah made a sand hill. Then she took Grandma's hand and went back to the water. "One more jump," said Hannah. Grandma said, "Ready?" They jumped at the very same time. Splash!

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
story:
Lydia stood in the reading corner. She held something new in her hand. It was her very first library card. It had her name on it.

"I want that dinosaur book!" she shouted. She jumped up and clapped her hands.

Then Lydia looked around. A boy sat on a big pillow. He was reading. A grandma was reading too. Their eyes went up, up to her loud voice. Lydia put her hands over her mouth. Oops.

She walked on her tippy toes. She found the dinosaur book on the shelf. She carried it to the desk very carefully. The librarian smiled and scanned her new card. Beep!

"You can keep it for next week too," the librarian whispered.

Lydia whispered back, "Next week I will get the robot book." She hugged the dinosaur book tight. Then she sat on a small red cushion. She turned page one. "Rawr," she whispered, very, very quietly. The reading boy smiled at her.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
Weston wanted a book about animals. He looked at the library shelf. The shelf was full of books. So many books! He pulled one out. It was about trucks. He put it back.

"Where are the animal books?" he asked. Miss Ana, the librarian, smiled. "Come with me," she said. "The books live in groups." They walked past a shelf of toy books. Then they walked past a shelf of food books. "Apples," said Weston. "And bread!"

Then Weston saw it. A whole shelf of animal books. "Look, look!" he said. He picked a big one. A lion was on the cover. He sat down on the floor to look. His friend Milo came over.

"I want a truck book," said Milo. Weston stood up. He knew just where to look! He took Milo's hand. They walked back to the shelf. Weston found a truck book. It had a big red truck on the cover.

Milo hugged the book. "You found it!" he said. "Listen," said Weston. "Books sit with their friends." Then he opened his lion book. The lion gave a big ROAR. Weston jumped. Then he laughed and laughed.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
story:
Sofia went to the library with Dad. On the craft table there was paper. There were circles, squares, and rectangles. There was a picture of a sailboat with a triangle sail.

Sofia wanted to make a sailboat. "Where is a triangle?" she asked. Dad looked in the box. There was no triangle paper. There was only a square.

Dad picked up the scissors. "Watch," he said. He cut from one corner to the opposite corner. The square fell open. Now there were two triangles! Sofia clapped her hands. "Two! One for me!"

She took one triangle. A boy named Leo got the other one. Leo smiled big. Sofia glued her triangle on her boat. It looked just like the picture in the song book. "Row, row, row your boat," she sang. Her loose tooth wiggled when she sang. Leo sang too, and their two boats sat side by side on the table.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
story:
Eleanor sat at the dinner table. She wanted her bedtime story now. "Can we read now, Mama?" she asked.

Mama said, "Now we eat dinner. The story comes later, after bath."

Eleanor looked at her plate. She took a small bite of rice. "Is it later now?" she asked.

"Not yet," said Mama. "Now is this moment. See? You are chewing right now."

Eleanor chewed. She watched Mama fold a napkin. The napkin went from bumpy to flat. "Now I drink," said Eleanor. She took a sip.

Papa said, "Yesterday we ate soup. Today we eat rice. Tomorrow we will eat pasta."

"I like pasta," said Eleanor. She ate more rice, one spoon at a time. She waited. She was brave about waiting.

At last the plate was empty. Bath came and went. Then Eleanor sat in her soft pajamas on the big bed.

"Now?" she asked.

Mama smiled. "Yes. Now is story time."

Eleanor snuggled close. "Read it now, all of it!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
story:
Madeline went to the park with her daddy. She wanted to paint a card for Grandma. The card needed a pink flower. But Madeline had no pink paint.

She looked around the park. One, two, three colors! She saw red paint, blue paint, yellow paint, and green paint. No pink anywhere. "I want pink," said Madeline.

She sat at the little paint table. She pushed her swing high first, then she got to work. Madeline put red paint on her brush. She painted a red flower. "Too red," she said. Grandma wanted pink.

Then Madeline had an idea. She took the white paint. She stirred white into the red. Round and round went the brush. The red turned lighter. It turned pink! Madeline looked and looked. "Pink!" she shouted. She painted the flower pink, pink, pink.

She folded the card carefully. Then she ran to show daddy. "A pink flower for Grandma!" said Madeline. Daddy said, "Grandma will love it." Madeline smiled big. Then she pointed at the grass. "Green!" she said. "Blue sky! Yellow sun!" And she danced all the way home.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: playing on a sports team for the season
story:
Rowan ran onto the basketball court. His shoes squeaked on the long, shiny floor. He was on a team this season. His sister sat with Mom on the bench. His team had five players. Five players, one ball.

Rowan got the ball. He threw it up. It hit the rim. It did not go in. He looked down at his shoes.

Then he heard voices. "Good try, Rowan!" his teammates called. "Try again!" They clapped for him. Rowan looked up. They were still clapping. "Can they cheer if I miss?" he asked his coach. "Watch and see," said the coach. The ball came back to Rowan. He threw it again. This time it went in. Swish. His teammates cheered even louder. His sister jumped up and down. After the game, Rowan waved to his team. "Same time next week?" he asked. "Same time," they said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: getting a first haircut at a salon
story:
Kinsley went to the mall with her dad. They were not late. "First haircut today!" said Dad. Kinsley held his hand tight.

The hairdresser smiled. "Sit here, please." Kinsley climbed up into the big chair. The hairdresser put a cape around her shoulders. It was blue and shiny. Snip, snip, snip went the scissors. Little bits of hair fell down. They landed on the cape. They did not get on her shirt. Not on her shoes. Not one bit.

Kinsley looked down. "The hairs slide off!" she said. She puffed out her chest like a superhero. "I am Cape Girl!" The hairdresser laughed. Dad laughed too. Snip, snip, snip. More hair slid down, down, down. It slid like a pig sliding in mud. Kinsley giggled and giggled. When they were done, she jumped down. "Cape Girl needs a snack," she said. Dad said, "Cape Girl gets a snack."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
story:
Penelope wanted to make pancakes for her family. Dad said, "We need the recipe." The recipe hung on the fridge door on a big card.

Penelope read the first step. "One cup of flour!" she said. Dad helped her pour it. Then she saw the next step. "One egg," she said. She cracked it in the bowl. The egg was a little smelly, and she giggled.

Penelope got excited and skipped a step. She did not put in the baking powder. Dad cooked the pancakes on the hot pan. Penelope watched from her stool.

The pancakes came out flat. "Oh no," said Penelope. Dad said, "Let's look again."

They read the card together, one step at a time. They found the missed step. They mixed a new bowl. Dad cooked them. The pancakes came out big and fluffy.

Her little brother, a small boy named Sam, clapped his hands. "Yum!" he said. The family ate them all up.
